exercises.name: Isometric Neck Flexion
exercises.form_cue: Press forehead into palm. Resist — don't let head move. Hold 5-10 sec.
exercises.why: Strengthens deep cervical flexors without moving the spine — safe for disc protrusion.

exercises.name: Isometric Neck Extension
exercises.form_cue: Press back of head into palm. Resist evenly. Hold 5-10 sec.
exercises.why: Builds posterior cervical strength to support the C5-6 segment.

exercises.name: Chin Tucks
exercises.form_cue: Sit tall. Draw chin straight back (double chin). Feel stretch at skull base. Do NOT tilt head down.
exercises.why: THE #1 exercise for C5-6 disc protrusion. Opens the intervertebral foramen by 7-13%, decompressing the C6 nerve root.

exercises.name: Cervical Retraction with Overpressure
exercises.form_cue: Perform chin tuck, then use fingertips to gently push chin further back. Hold 3 sec.
exercises.why: Active decompression of the C5-6 foramen — the advanced chin tuck.

exercises.name: Scapular Squeezes
exercises.form_cue: Pinch shoulder blades together and DOWN. Hold 5 sec. Don't shrug.
exercises.why: Addresses upper back trigger points and supports the cervical-elbow kinetic chain.

exercises.name: Prone Y-T-W Raises
exercises.form_cue: Face-down on bed, arms hanging off edge. Raise arms into Y, then T, then W. Thumbs up. Light or no weight.
exercises.why: Scapular stabilizer activation — reduces compensatory tension causing trigger points.

exercises.name: Upper Trapezius Stretch
exercises.form_cue: Tilt head away from tight side. Gentle hand overpressure. STOP if radiating pain. Focus on LEFT side.
exercises.why: Releases the dominant left-sided trigger points identified in your referral.

exercises.name: Wrist Extensor Stretch
exercises.form_cue: Straighten left arm, palm down. Use right hand to gently press hand down. Feel stretch on outer forearm.
exercises.why: Stretches the common extensor tendon at the lateral epicondyle — the primary site of tennis elbow pain.

exercises.name: Wrist Flexor Stretch
exercises.form_cue: Straighten left arm, palm up. Use right hand to press fingers back toward you.
exercises.why: Balances the forearm musculature and reduces tension through the elbow joint.

exercises.name: Eccentric Wrist Extensions
exercises.form_cue: Rest forearm on table, wrist over edge, palm down. Use other hand to lift wrist up. Slowly lower under control (3 sec). Start with no weight.
exercises.why: The gold standard for lateral epicondylitis rehab. Eccentric loading stimulates tendon healing and remodeling.

exercises.name: Forearm Supination/Pronation
exercises.form_cue: Hold light object (hammer handle). Slowly rotate forearm palm-up then palm-down. Keep elbow at side.
exercises.why: Strengthens the rotator muscles of the forearm that support the lateral epicondyle.

exercises.name: Gentle Grip Squeezes
exercises.form_cue: Squeeze a soft ball or rolled towel. Hold 3 sec. Release. No pain allowed during this exercise.
exercises.why: Maintains grip strength while respecting the healing tendon. Pain-free grip work promotes blood flow.

exercises.name: Dead Bugs
exercises.form_cue: Lie on back, arms up, knees at 90°. Slowly extend opposite arm and leg. Keep lower back pressed to floor.
exercises.why: Safe core activation that doesn't load the cervical spine. Builds the deep stabilizers.

exercises.name: Bird Dogs
exercises.form_cue: On all fours, extend opposite arm and leg. Hold 5 sec. Keep hips level — don't rotate.
exercises.why: Trains the posterior chain and anti-rotation stability without spinal compression.

exercises.name: Glute Bridges
exercises.form_cue: Lie on back, feet flat, hip-width. Push hips up by squeezing glutes. Hold 3 sec at top.
exercises.why: Glute activation reduces compensatory loading through the lower back and supports future running.

exercises.name: Pallof Hold (Band)
exercises.form_cue: Stand sideways to anchor. Press band straight out from chest. Hold — resist rotation. 20 sec each side.
exercises.why: Anti-rotation strength is critical for running mechanics and spinal stability.

exercises.name: Bodyweight Squats
exercises.form_cue: Feet shoulder-width. Sit back and down. Knees track over toes. Chest up. Go as low as comfortable.
exercises.why: Foundation movement for running. Builds quad, glute, and ankle strength.

exercises.name: Step-Ups
exercises.form_cue: Use a sturdy step (15-20cm). Step up with one foot, drive through heel. Alternate legs.
exercises.why: Unilateral leg strength mimics running mechanics. Identifies left/right imbalances.

exercises.name: Calf Raises
exercises.form_cue: Stand on edge of step. Rise up on toes, hold 2 sec, slowly lower below step level.
exercises.why: Calf strength is the #1 predictor of running injury resilience. 20 reps builds endurance.

exercises.name: Hip Flexor Stretch
exercises.form_cue: Half-kneeling position. Push hips forward. Squeeze glute of back leg. Feel stretch in front of hip.
exercises.why: Desk workers have tight hip flexors that inhibit glute activation and alter running gait.

exercises.name: Single Leg Balance
exercises.form_cue: Stand on one leg. Eyes open. Hold 30 sec each side. Progress to eyes closed when stable.
exercises.why: Proprioception training for ankle stability and fall prevention during running.

exercises.name: Towel Toe Curls
exercises.form_cue: Place towel on floor. Scrunch toes to pull towel toward you. Release and repeat.
exercises.why: Strengthens the intrinsic foot muscles — your natural arch support for running.

exercises.name: Ankle Circles
exercises.form_cue: Seated. Lift foot off ground. Draw large circles with toes. 15 clockwise, 15 counter-clockwise each foot.
exercises.why: Ankle mobility is essential for running. Prevents stiffness that leads to compensatory injuries.

exercises.name: Short Foot Exercise
exercises.form_cue: Seated, foot flat. Try to shorten your foot by pulling ball of foot toward heel WITHOUT curling toes. Hold 5 sec.
exercises.why: Activates the arch muscles that support midfoot strike running form.
